a16z's Martin Casado on the four mindsets people bring to investing, and why knowing yours stops you from justifying your own bias:

1. Financial

"The correct proxy for the health of a business is the market it's going into and its finances. That's what it is. What are the SaaS metrics? What is the size of the market? That is a proxy for the entire business."

2. Productive

"You believe you're investing in a productive asset, and the productive asset is what's creating value. If you believe in that, as it creates value, it will create market... The type of diligence you do if you're a productive investor is more like, what is the technical approach? What are the adjacent markets?"

3. Frontier

"I think this is the romantic, idealized version of VC from the 60s and 70s, which is kind of YOLO. It's like, founders know better than VCs, and they've seen something that I don't see, and they're gonna go out there and do it. And, like, who am I to second guess them?"

4. Speculative

"It is always so surprising how prevalent it is... They don't even care about the asset. They just want to time a market, right?... They're like, 'Well, this looks cheap. It's clearly gonna go up in value' or, 'This is the top of the market, like, I'm gonna get out.'"

"...You can justify any deal or not justify any deal. So if you don't know what your beliefs are, you'll always basically just kind of justify whatever personal bias you have."

@martin_casado w/ @patrick_oshag on @InvestLikeBest

I can only reply to a minority of comments, and it’s usually luck-of-the-draw what I see when I’m online. And Twitter isn’t really the best place for long-form debates.

“Why do you think the legal system couldn’t prevent the Biden Admin from allowing millions of unknown foreign men to illegally enter the country?”

-Surely you’re aware of the asymmetry that courts are more able to block specific illegal actions than force officials to take positive actions that require funding. In other words, with a stroke of a pen a court can say,“no, those tariffs are illegal actually, you can’t use emergency powers for indefinite and broad new taxes” but it’s much harder to say, “you have to allocate more resources to the border.” To fix the latter you generally need an executive and legislative branch with the will to do it, which is partially what the 2024 election was a mandate on.

“Why can’t the legal system prevent criminals who’ve been arrested 37 times from being let back into society?”

-Places where people are arrested 37 times tend to be cities where the politicians and courts are in agreement. That’s the set of policies they have on the books and how the rules are being interpreted. If people get fed up with it they can elect people that will write and interpret stricter laws and sentences about repeated crime.

“Why couldn’t the legal system prevent billions of dollars of egregious welfare fraud?”

-Tons of cases are prosecuted each year. Even so, outright fraud is a small share of the spending. The bigger issue is healthcare bloat and demographics.

“Why can’t the legal system enact voter ID which is the most obvious and basic tenet of election security?”

-It’s not the role of the legal system to enact voter ID or other details around voting. That’s primarily within the legislative branch (unless the legislative branch does something that violates the Constitution).

“If you are so willing to label Trump a "fascist", perhaps you could assign a label to the people who fail to deliver the most basic functions of government? What label should they be given?”

-By definition, that description would be closer to anarchist.

Huge relief for $MARA.

FERC approved $MARA’s Long Ridge acquisition today (EC26-92). Good to see the IMM’s spurious BlackRock/Vanguard challenge get the Heisman. FERC also turned down the request to condition approval on keeping the plant’s output in PJM. Solid.

The deal: $1.512B enterprise value for ~0.5 GW of gas generation (485 MW authorized, 505 MW nameplate) and ~$144M of annualized adj. EBITDA, about 10.5x. Recent PJM gas plant deals went at about 7x (Talen 6.7x, Vistra 7x, NRG 7.5x), which would put the plant alone at ~$1.0B. MARA is paying ~$0.5B more for the land, gas wells, rail and expansion option. MARA keeps ~$900M of Long Ridge debt in place and needs ~$610M of cash, which the $600M of BTC-backed loans it drew in August are meant to cover. I’d expect it to close by the Nov 30 outside date.

Debt math: ~$1.9B of MARA’s $2.3B convert stack is zero coupon, so total post-close cash interest is roughly $140M: ~$58M on the Coinbase and Two Prime loans, ~$76M on Long Ridge’s own debt (the 8.75% notes alone are $52.5M) and ~$7M on the converts. Judging the deal on its own: the debt that finances it (Long Ridge’s ~$76M plus ~$46M on the new BTC loans) costs ~$123M a year against $144M of EBITDA, about 1.2x. The upside is expansion.

MARA talks about 600 gross MW of AI load at the site. That appears to include the existing 200 MW of grid load (on top of the 505 MW plant that sells into PJM). AEP’s 2025 filing proposed reconductoring the feeder serving a customer at the Hannibal station to go from 100 to 200 MW, for about $0.5M, targeting about nine months from PJM first seeing the need to in-service. The station ties into four 138 kV lines and once fed a 540 MW smelter, which is encouraging, but nothing is signed. To get from 200 to 600 MW, AEP would likely need to add a second feed or upgrade lines, or MARA would build on-site generation, which raises turbine availability questions. I can’t find a public study of how much more the grid connection can carry. AEP Ohio’s data center tariff also requires large customers to pay for at least 85% of contracted capacity for up to 12 years, if it applies here. Still, an energized site with fuel, land and a 138 kV hub may beat waiting in ERCOT’s queue.

It’s unclear whether the Hannibal buildout goes through the Starwood JV, where MARA would keep up to 50%. That will decide how much of the 600 MW upside MARA owns. Each 100MW developed at a 7% cap rate and $2M/MW rent could be $1.5B+ of value creation, so it's a big variable and explains why they paid ~$500M above the 7x multiple for the extra capacity.

Next catalyst, possibly at closing or just after: a signed lease.
